body_markdown:
Emerson wrote that it’s a luxury to be understood. But from the front seat of a Bentley Flying Spur Mulliner, you’d find it quite hard to agree with Ralph.


No, luxury is a feeling of ease at 157 mph. Of wafting along a Big Sky mountain two-lane and approaching the sound barrier without an iota of rushing atmosphere buffeting against the acoustic glass. Luxury is unstressed, a burly hybrid V-8 humming assuredly underhood and an avocado-green leather seat so sublime and supple, your heart melts like Dali’s clock when your back presses against it.


Bentley


Bentley


Bentley


If I won the lottery, there would be signs, as the kids say. Stop one is the doughnut shop. Stop two is the Bentley dealer.


As a perpetually undermonied car writer (there’s not a single sock in my drawer without a hole in the heel), the aforementioned Bentley media drive in rural Montana set my personal high-water mark for ultra luxury. Modern Bentleys reinforce many notions about old-world sensibilities, but the key is how they make drivers feel special; in a Bentley Mulliner, the interior fittings are so plainly fine, you feel among the landed gentry. Even with holes in your socks.


For hundreds of years, that’s what luxury has meant in the material sense: the acquisition of (or aspiration to) items or experiences which, through their quality and finery, elevate life from the mundane.


Bentley


Maybe that’s why I’m so fascinated by what’s going on over at Jaguar. The company itself is trying to regain its composure after a freefall that arguably began some time in the ’70s.


With some luck, Jag’s current state of affairs—no new cars,[a convoluted rebrand](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-reinvention-of-jaguar-needs-a-miracle-to-succeed/) , promises of an electric ultra-luxury repositioning—is just the bottom of a yo-yo’s arc. Will we look back at this moment as the start of a magnificent and rapid ascension?


Jaguar Type 01


Jaguar


Bentley Flying Spur Mulliner


Bentley


By now, you’ve seen photos of the brand’s hail-mary pass at resurrection,[the Type 01](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/jaguars-controversial-concept-car-stops-paris-traffic/) . Unlike the Bentley’s rounded and refined lines, the Jag cuts a sharp and brutish figure, confident and brawling. It is the Bentley’s spiritual antithesis. The Jag is Daniel Craig to Crewe’s Brosnan.


Nowhere is this divergence clearer than when you line up the Bentley’s interior against that of the production Jaguar Type 01,[which was unveiled earlier this month](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/jaguar-shows-off-its-past-and-previews-its-future-in-pebble-beach/) . So what has Jaguar staked its company’s future on? Well, it’s this:


Jaguar


You could charitably describe the Type 01’s interior as clean. Or perhaps minimalistic. Personally, it reminds me of a very specific type of café that exists all across Seoul, South Korea. These spaces are sparse and muted, yet somehow warm. Incredible cortados on the bar and an unblinking, expressionless barista to take your order.


But is it *luxurious* ? To my eyes, no. Or at least not according to my definition of the word. Just don’t mistake Jaguar’s restraint for lack of effort. This is a very thoroughly and intentionally designed interior, and the proof will be in the real-life experience, not images. Someone who believes luxury is the inside of a Korean hipster coffee spot would feel transported here.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Through one lens you could see the Type 01’s departure from the traditional, wood-trimmed trappings of luxury—Bentley or midcentury Jag being a prime example—as an act of desperation. Jaguar has been on that glide path for decades, moored as it was to a golden era of performance and design that it could never quite translate into the modern age. Bucking off all that expectation is, in that light, a sensible strategy.


1954 Jaguar XK 120 SE


Hagerty Media


Jaguar Type 01


Jaguar


But that doesn’t explain Ferrari, which released its own departure from curl-your-toes-it’s-so-fine luxury. It’s called the[Luce](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/ferrari-luce-design-conventional-or-intentional/) , the brand’s first all-electric vehicle. Ferrari, however, is quite unlike Jaguar in that Maranello’s business is the envy of every car company on Earth. (Note that, in the ’50s, Ferrari and Jaguar’s fortunes were somewhat reversed.) In this context, the Luce’s arrival felt a lot more like a brashly confident move than some flavor of desperation.


Despite the resounding echoes of *“ThAt’S nOt A rEaL fErRari!”* from the keyboard quarterbacks, Ferrari says it has sold out of the Luce’s 2026 production (just under 500 examples). Adding to the drama is the first production Ferrari Luce that sold at a recent Monterey charity auction—for a cool $40 million. Prior to that sale, if someone MadLib’d a headline that started with “Rich bidder plunks down $40 mil on Ferrari **__** ,” nobody would have filled in the blank by scrawling, “EV with the silhouette of a Logitech gaming mouse.”


Ferrari


Ferrari


Ferrari


What does all this tell us about the state of luxury cars in 2026? That at least two competitors are hedging on a bifurcation of the ultra-luxe market. Rather than a Bentley’s classicism, Ferrari and Jag are betting on a sparse, hyper-clean aesthetic that companies like Kia, Hyundai, and Tesla have already embraced.


Hard to imagine the same scenario 20 years ago, the upper-crust taking cues from volume sellers instead of the opposite. (And in case you think that’s a put-down, I truly believe the South Koreans have led global vehicle design for roughly the last decade.)


So why the sudden flip?


My gut tells me that, perhaps, “The West” is now importing certain sensibilities, rather than purely exporting them. You see it in the boxy fit of our clothing, in your kid neighbor’s K-Pop Demon Hunters obsession, and in our cars.


Ferrari


During an interview for another outlet, one program manager at a major luxury company told me in confidence that they were increasingly looking to China to spot future trends, from interior layouts to exterior character. So are the company’s customers. The Chinese domestic car industry, this person explained, can iterate its designs much more quickly than Western counterparts, which march to a slower, more conservative cadence. Hefty government subsidies, looser regulations, workplace culture, and a billion other factors can explain it all away, but it seems that the speed at which the Chinese market moves—for better or worse—has shifted the tide.


The future doesn’t live on our shores in this moment. Jaguar and Ferrari see a huge market in China and the Middle East, and they’ve identified the zeitgeist. The Luce’s interior, designed by Apple veteran Jony Ive’s firm, is Ferrari’s way of putting out feelers into this space. Jaguar, which can’t afford half measures at the moment, is leaping headlong to seize it with the Type 01. If luxury is intended to elevate us from the mundane with purpose, the Luce and Type 01 propose something else: elevating the purposefully mundane.


Ferrari Luce


Ferrari


Jaguar Type 01


Jaguar


From an outsider’s standpoint, it’s a fascinating proposition. Of course, I have no skin in the game. For myself and the rest of the holes-in-socks set, it doesn’t matter much whether the Luce sinks or swims. Same with the Jag. I don’t aspire to own either and may be too old-fashioned and unenlightened to fully understand them. Ignorance, I suppose, is a luxury all its own.


***


*The only car writer dumb brave enough to flip a grain truck on its roof, Kyle Kinard once plied his trade at America’s greatest car magazines. He now lives near Seattle and enjoys the rain. His column,[Kinardi Line](https://www.hagerty.com/media/category/opinion/kinardi-line/) , runs monthly, as does the[Camaro vs. World project-car series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/camaro-vs-world/) .*
